title: Food Access Research Atlas
content:
Updated: 7/27/2026

Contact: Alana Rhone

Overview

The Food Access Research Atlas (FARA) includes two measures of retail food access, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM) and the Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM). Together, these mapping tools present indicators of food access for low-income and other census tracts using different measures of food retailer accessibility.

These measures can help highlight neighborhoods where distance and transportation barriers may limit access to food retailers. Limited access can influence which stores people can reach, the time and cost required to travel, and how often households are able to shop.

What can you do with the Atlas?

Create and compare maps showing food access indicators by census tract using two mapping applications, each offering different measures of food retailer accessibility: SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM) Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM);

SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM)

Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM);

Compare food access measures based on straight-line (Euclidean) and driving (road network) distance;

View indicators of food access for selected populations; and

Download census-tract-level data on food access measures.

Objectives

Limited access to food sources may make it harder for some people to eat a healthy diet. There are many ways to measure food store access for individuals and neighborhoods. Most measures and definitions consider at least some of the following factors:

Geographic proximity to a store or the number of stores in a given area;

Individual-level resources, such as family income or vehicle availability; and

Neighborhood-level resources, such as the neighborhood’s average income and the availability of public transportation.

In the Food Access Research Atlas, low‑income census tracts are defined based on their poverty rates or median family income, and low access refers to being far from a SNAP‑authorized retailer or a large food retailer (supermarkets, supercenters, and large grocery stores).

FARA provides two mapping applications to describe food access along these dimensions, each designed to capture different indicators of geographic access to food, drawing on multiple data sources and methodologies: SNAP‑authorized stores (which include a wide range of retailer formats such as specialty food stores, combination grocery/other stores, convenience stores, small and medium groceries, large groceries, supermarkets, and super stores) and large grocers (supercenters, supermarkets, and large grocery stores).
